content.text: RH134 · Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 · Beginner-friendly lesson
This chapter teaches you how to control what happens when Linux starts, recover access when the root password is lost, and repair file-system problems that stop the system from booting.
When you press the power button, Linux does not become ready instantly. Several steps happen in order.
Checks hardware and finds a bootable device.
Shows the boot menu and selects a Linux kernel.
Starts the Linux core and prepares the system to access its root file system.
Starts system services and brings the system to its target.
The system is ready for users.
This is firmware built into the computer. It starts when you power on the machine, checks basic hardware, and looks for a bootable device.
GRUB2 is the boot loader. It lets you choose a Linux kernel to start.
Think of it as the first menu you see before Linux fully starts.

Its configuration is generated from files such as /etc/default/grub and scripts in /etc/grub.d/. The generated configuration is commonly stored at /boot/grub2/grub.cfg on RHEL 8 BIOS-based systems; UEFI systems can use a different configuration path.
The kernel is the central part of Linux. It manages memory, processes, hardware, and other essential resources.
This is a temporary early-boot environment. It contains tools and drivers Linux may need before it can access the real root file system.
systemd is the system manager that starts services and moves Linux into its intended operating state.
For example, it can start networking, logging, and login services.
A target is a named operating state that groups together the services and other units required for a particular purpose.
Think of targets as different modes for the server.
The most important targets in this chapter are:
Multi-user system with a graphical login interface
Minimal emergency environment for serious problems
A graphical target includes the multi-user target, along with the additional requirements for graphical operation.
This means Linux is configured to boot to the multi-user target by default.

Only targets that allow isolation can be used with isolate.

sections.title: 3. Boot into a different target for one time

content.text: Sometimes Linux cannot start normally because a service or configuration is broken. You may want to start in rescue or emergency mode instead.
You can change the target for a single boot from the GRUB2 menu.
When the GRUB2 menu appears, select the normal Linux entry.
Press e to edit the entry.
Find the line that starts with linux.

6. Press Ctrl+x to boot with the change.
This change applies to that boot only. It does not permanently change the default target.
Rescue mode: Starts more of the system, including basic initialization. It is useful for repairing configuration problems.
Emergency mode: Starts a more minimal environment. The root file system is normally mounted read-only.
If you need to repair /etc/fstab in emergency mode, you may first need to remount the root file system as read/write. We will cover that below.
The root account is the Linux administrator account with extensive control over the system.
If you lose its password and cannot log in through another administrator account, RHEL 8 provides a recovery method using the boot loader.
Practice this only on your own lab VM or an authorized machine. It requires console access and should not be attempted on a computer you do not administer.
Find the line beginning with linux.
The system pauses in an early boot environment and gives you a root shell.
Step 2: Make the real root file system writable
mount works with mounted file systems.
remount changes the options of a file system that is already mounted.
/sysroot is where the real system's root file system is mounted during this recovery stage.
chroot makes /sysroot act as the root directory for the commands you run inside it. This lets you change the password belonging to the installed system rather than the temporary recovery environment.
Step 4: Set a new root password
Follow the prompts to enter and confirm the new password.

touch creates an empty file if it does not exist. In this procedure, the file tells RHEL to relabel file security contexts during the next boot. This is important because the password-reset process may create a file without the correct SELinux label.
The first exit leaves the chroot environment. The second leaves the early boot shell.
The system continues booting, performs the SELinux relabel, and may reboot again automatically.
Do not try these commands on your normal working installation just for practice; use a disposable VM and take a snapshot first.

sections.title: 5. Read logs from a previous boot

content.text: Sometimes Linux fails during startup and then reboots. Logs can help you find the reason.
journalctl displays system logs. The -b option limits the output to the current boot.
View logs from the previous boot
The -1 means the boot before the current one.
To display only errors from that previous boot:
Here, -p err filters the output to errors and more severe messages.

Important: Previous-boot logs are available only if the system retained them. By default, logs may be stored under /run/log/journal, which is cleared after reboot. Persistent logging can be configured using /etc/systemd/journald.conf.
Check jobs that are stuck during startup
This shows systemd jobs that are running or waiting. A job that cannot complete may delay other jobs.

sections.title: 6. Repair file-system problems that prevent booting

content.text: This is one of the most practical sections for a Linux administrator.
Linux reads /etc/fstab to learn which file systems should be mounted. If this file contains a mistake, the system may fail to boot normally.
What kinds of mistakes cause problems?

Automatic repair may fail, leading to emergency mode

Step 3: Remount the root file system as writable
The / symbol represents the root of the Linux file-system tree.
This attempts to mount the applicable file systems listed in /etc/fstab that are not already mounted.

If there are no errors, reboot:
The system should now boot normally if the corrected entry was the cause of the problem.
The nofail option in /etc/fstab allows booting to continue when a particular file system fails to mount.
It can be appropriate for optional storage, such as a nonessential external disk. But using it for required storage may allow applications to start without the files they need.
Starts basic system initialization and is useful for repairing system configuration or services.
Starts a more minimal environment. The root file system is typically read-only, so you may need to remount it before making changes.
Pauses the boot process in the initramfs, before the real system takes over. This is the method used in the textbook's root-password reset procedure.
Need a basic maintenance environment? Consider rescue mode.
Need to investigate a serious early boot or file-system issue? Consider emergency mode.
Lost the root password? Use the authorized boot-loader recovery procedure with rd.break.
